source.title: UrbanVerse: Scaling Urban Simulation by Watching City-Tour Videos
source.authors: Mingxuan Liu; Hong-Lin He; Elisa Ricci; Wayne Wu; Bo-Lei Zhou

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure and table text is flattened, and the fitted exponents in the Fig. 9 plots are garbled in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: Extends power-law scaling claims to reinforcement-learned urban navigation policies, measuring generalization error as the number of training layouts or digital-cousin scenes increases.
record.gate_note: The paper measures policy success as training-scene scale changes and reports power-law fits. Its other policy benchmarks do not test scaling relationships and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: Fits a power law to held-out test error (1 − success rate) of PPO navigation policies against training-data scale (layouts, digital cousins). This is a new regime for V5: RL policy data scaling. The measure is task error, not pretraining loss, and it has nothing to do with downstream use of a pretrained model, so V6 does not apply.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that policies trained on UrbanVerse scenes show power-law data scaling in test error with more layouts and more digital cousins. They add that procedurally generated scenes scale poorly, which they attribute to their lack of real-world diversity. They also say real-grounded scenes enable generalization to unseen simulated and real environments.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales RL navigation policies by training-scene layouts and digital-cousin variants, measuring success-rate error. It does not scale language models, parameters, tokens, compute, or held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies two training-scale measures: number of layouts and number of digital cousins per layout. It reports better overall performance on AutoBench than CraftBench, but the cited power-law fit correlations are for the plotted CraftBench fits.

fits_no_version.finding: With matched layout counts, policies trained on procedurally generated UrbanSim scenes improve very little as layouts increase, while policies trained on UrbanVerse real-grounded scenes improve sharply.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-scaling gains in embodied RL depend on how realistic the training data distribution is.

record.problems: The policy scaling evidence is for one navigation setup and uses success-rate error rather than language-model loss. The extracted Fig. 9 fit exponents are garbled, and uncertainty estimates for the scaling fits are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Overall benchmark comparisons in Tables 3–4 and other navigation results were left out because they do not report scale-dependent results.

untested.parts: All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: no compute-optimal allocation; model size is never varied.
Image/video model loss, repeated data, fine-tuning/transfer scaling, and parameter or compute scaling. Only training-scene count is varied.
All: no downstream-task performance tied to scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting methods or setups for exponents.

missing.what: PPO-UrbanSim (PG) success rate vs number of training layouts; described as very limited improvement
AutoBench success rate vs number of digital cousins (higher than CraftBench; gap narrows)
Fitted power-law exponents and coefficients (E = β N^−α) for layouts and cousins; garbled in extracted text

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence for a scaling law: few points, short ranges, only Pearson r reported, no uncertainty, and the exponent is unreadable. The paper is primarily a simulator/dataset paper. The scaling section is a small validation of data scaling, citing Lin et al. 2025b rather than Kaplan/Hoffmann's loss form.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of model parameters and tokens.
Effects of model depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The study tests power-law-shaped scaling for RL policy generalization with training-scene scale. It does not test image or video model loss, repeated data, or fine-tuning and transfer as scaling regimes.
The study measures urban-navigation policy success, not general downstream task performance or its relationship to language-model pretraining loss.
Whether exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with fitting choices or setup, or whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: PPO-UrbanVerse
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of unique training layouts and fitted test error against layout count.

conditions.value: N ∈ {1, 8, 16, 32} layouts, corresponding to 5, 40, 80, and 160 scenes
test error E = 1 − SR; power-law fit

rows.measure: Pearson correlation for the log–log power-law fit of test error against number of training layouts
rows.note: The authors state that the log–log fit confirms power-law behavior. The fitted exponent is not recoverable from the extracted figure text.
rows.check: Unlink V6: success on held-out scenes is the training task itself, not downstream performance tied to scale or pretraining loss. The value is a Pearson r from a 4-point log–log fit (N=1–32, about 1.5 decades). It shows fit quality, not the exponent, which is garbled. The text also notes a flat slope at small N.

rows.subject: PPO-UrbanVerse
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of digital cousins per layout and fitted test error against cousin count.

conditions.value: m ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} digital cousins per layout, using 32 layouts
10 AutoBench scenes and 10 CraftBench scenes; Fig. 9(d) identifies CraftBench
test error E = 1 − SR; power-law fit

rows.measure: Pearson correlation for the log–log power-law fit of test error against number of digital cousins
rows.note: The authors state that the log–log fit confirms power-law behavior and that success rate increases as cousin count grows. The fitted exponent is not recoverable from the extracted figure text.
rows.check: Unlink V6. The fit covers only m=1–5 cousins (under one decade) and 5 points, on CraftBench only. AutoBench was measured (Fig. 9b) but not fitted. The exponent is unreadable and only Pearson r is given.

relationships.condition: PPO navigation policies trained on UrbanVerse real-grounded scenes, CraftBench test error vs layouts (1–32) and cousins (1–5)
relationships.reason: Log–log fits of test error give Pearson r −0.930 (R1) and −0.903 (R2); authors call it clear power-law behaviour.
relationships.display_finding: Log-log test-error fits yield Pearson r = −0.930 for layouts and −0.903 for cousins, described as power-law behavior.

relationships.condition: Narrow scale ranges, and procedurally generated (UrbanSim) training scenes
relationships.reason: The fits span only about 1.5 and under 1 decade with 4–5 points (R1, R2), and the text notes a flat slope at small N. From the text, PG-trained policies show 'very limited improvement' with more layouts, so scaling depends on data realism. That result is unfitted and has no row.
relationships.display_finding: Fits covered about 1.5 and less than one decade with 4–5 points, slopes flattened at small model sizes, and procedurally trained policies improved very little with additional layouts.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
